reason: Attacked and survived, and the verifier's correction is the right way round. I checked the spelling against two transcriptions that descend from the engraved plates rather than from a later reprint. The Wikisource text of The Marriage of Heaven and Hell, which follows the illuminated book at copy D, prints In seed time learn, in harvest teach, in winter enjoy. as the first line under Proverbs of Hell, with no hyphen, and gives the second proverb as Drive your cart and your plow over the bones of the dead, with plow and not plough. The Academy of American Poets text of Proverbs of Hell prints the same first line with the same unhyphenated seed time and the same plow. Two independent transcriptions of Blake's own text agreeing on the disputed character is enough to defeat the hyphen, and the hyphenated seed-time together with plough is the fingerprint of a later printed setting, which is what the verifier identified in the 1906 John W. Luce edition of Boston behind the original proposal. Erdman's standard text is cited in the secondary literature with the unhyphenated reading as well. The locator holds: the Proverbs of Hell begin on plate 7, after the close of the first Memorable Fancy, and this is the first of them. Attribution is Blake's own engraved work, not a reported or collected saying, and the misattribution list has no Blake trap. shipped.js returns no hit and no near-hit, Blake stands at 0 of 3 for the year, is not banned, and appears in no carry-in, so there is no twice-in-the-month collision. Scope is clean: engraved 1790, no scripture despite the infernal framing, no proverb-of-unknown-origin problem since this one has a named author and a plate number, and nothing needing a content warning. Tag Poetry is right for the form: the Marriage is an illuminated prophetic book, catalogued and anthologised as Blake's poetry, and the Proverbs are printed as one proverb to a line, so quoting one line as one line does not break the verse rule. The quotation ends in a full stop, uses no quote marks at all so the curly-quote rule is not engaged, and the source line leads with the name, carries no dash and runs 99 characters. The note carries no dash either and says plainly what was changed and why.

residual: The date. The source line gives (1790), which is the date on Blake's own title page and the conventional one, but the book was engraved and coloured over several years and the copy the verifier followed for the spelling, copy D, is dated about 1795. The card is not wrong to print 1790, but the note would be more honest if it said the wording follows the engraved text rather than a printed edition, since as it stands the source line names no edition at all for the words it ships and rests entirely on plate 7 as the locator. Second, Poetry is the defensible tag but the Proverbs themselves are prose aphorisms, so an editor who wanted Philosophy here would not be obviously wrong.
